title: On Death and Donuts
html:
“A life, if well lived, is long enough.” —Seneca

In November 2022, I conducted an experiment that I dubbed “No Dopamine November.” For the duration of the month, I cut out podcasts, audiobooks, YouTube videos, and music—things I used to numb myself. For 30 days, I was entirely alone with my thoughts.

To say it was a strange experience is an understatement. On just the second day of NDN, I had the following text exchange with a friend [with minor grammatical edits for clarity] :

Me: “Only day 2 and am currently pondering how people’s generally held desire to continue living/live longer might be based on an illusion🥲. And may therefore be unjustifiable.”

Friend: “Do you mean to push to increase lifespan? What’s the illusion?”

Me: “Yes. Or just people near the end of their life who want just a few more days. I think there’s this feeling that goes unarticulated that if we just get a bit more time, THEN we’ll be satisfied. It’s the illusion that satisfaction can be sustained. It’s the very same feeling that drives us towards money or status, only to realize that attaining those things doesn’t bring the relief from life’s intrinsic unsatisfactoriness that we had hoped it would. It’s the same chronic goalpost shifting, but scaled up all the way to life itself😂😅. No, it doesn’t seem like more life will make u more satisfied. Also, all these thoughts are super half-baked soooooo…. take them as such😂”

Friend: “Oh god. Felt a little bit of tightening in my chest, which at least tells me there’s something there…”

“Chronic goalpost shifting, but scaled up all the way to life itself.”

😵‍💫😵‍💫😵‍💫😵‍💫😵‍💫😵‍💫😵‍💫😵‍💫😵‍💫😵‍💫😵‍💫😵‍💫😵‍💫😵‍💫😵‍💫😵‍💫😵‍💫😵‍💫😵‍💫😵‍💫😵‍💫😵‍💫😵‍💫😵‍💫😵‍💫😵‍💫😵‍💫😵‍💫😵‍💫😵‍💫😵‍💫😵‍💫😵‍💫😵‍💫😵‍💫😵‍💫😵‍💫😵‍💫

It’s like Jim Carrey’s quote on being rich and famous, but rebranded to be more nauseating.

Carrey says:

“I think everybody should get rich and famous and do everything they ever dreamed of so they can see that it’s not the answer.” —Jim Carrey

My version would be something like:

“I think everybody should be able to live forever so they can realize that they’ll be just as unsatisfied at 500 years old as they were at 50.” —Nov. 2022 Charlie

At bottom, it’s the same message. Getting what you want isn’t satisfying, even if all you want is one more day with your parents, spouse, or kids. It’s never enough.

This is the human condition.

If, for some reason, you’re not convinced by either me or Jim Carrey, then let me give you an example that you can almost certainly relate to—eating donuts. Imagine you’ve just finished dinner. Now, it’s donut time. As you open the box and your eyes dance upon the mosaic of calorically dense, colorful carbs, your salivary glands go into hyperdrive. Drooling, you sink your teeth into the fluffy goodness. Your brain floods with dopamine. It’s amazing… for maybe two seconds. Then, it’s great. Then, it’s just okay. By the time you’re on your last bite, the joy has vanished, and finishing the donut is more akin to a chore than it is to an ultimate indulgence. And have you noticed what happens when you finally finish it? The last bite doesn’t compare to the first, but even though it fell short of your expectations, you’re still craving one more. And now you’re feeling a bit empty.

Highs are always accompanied by lows, and the depth of the lows is always proportional to the height of the highs. There is a reason why gold medalists so often struggle with feelings of depression and a loss of purpose. The bigger they are, the harder they fall.

This pain-pleasure duality is ever-present in our experience, yet we’re so eager to ignore it—doing things that are bound to disappoint us. If you ask someone if having more money will finally make them happy, most people will probably say no. And yet, they pursue greater wealth. If you ask someone if one more bite of a donut will forever quench their craving for donuts, most people will probably say no. And yet, they’re always tempted to take one more. Many of us are aware that short-term monetary or caloric gains won’t give us a persistent sense of peace and contentment, yet we pursue them anyway.

It makes sense that so many contemplative traditions emphasize detachment from material possessions and resistance to indulgence. For thousands of years, people have recognized that those things don’t guarantee contentment, and, at the extremes, will likely make you miserable.

But far fewer philosophers argue that the desire to live longer is misguided. Some, like Seneca, might claim that life is plenty long if we live it well, but I’ve yet to come across a philosopher who draws the connection between the hedonic treadmill and wanting more life (though I’m sure someone somewhere probably has). I believe the difficulty in connecting the two lies in our misperception of the marginal utility of days. Put simply, we think more life is better because we overestimate how much value a given day will add to our lives. We can project ourselves onto our deathbeds and think of how much we would give for just one more day, but what if we got that extra day? We’d be right back where we started, wanting just one more day. And the treadmill continues.

Just as we were not satisfied with one more bite of donut, or one more pay raise, we won’t be satisfied with one more day. We overestimate the value of adding extra days to the end of our lives because, at the end of our lives, days are a scarce resource. Framing certain days as your last can certainly make them special, but if our number of “final days” keeps growing, then days are no longer scarce, and one more day of life tomorrow won’t make you any more satisfied than you were by the one more day of life that you lived out today. “Enough” is a mirage on the horizon. The closer you get to it, the further back it moves.

Humans are programmed to want more—to be dissatisfied by default. Being dissatisfied is adaptive. It’s one of the reasons we’re so successful as a species. But we evolved to reproduce, not to be content. Contentment requires learning to want what you already have, or, to take it one step further, not wanting anything at all. That’s Buddhism in a nutshell.

In summary, we don’t want to live longer because it’s good for us. We want to live longer because we’re confused—because we’re falling prey to the same ancient brain circuitry that drives us towards money and donuts. More donuts won’t make you happy, nor will more life. Life is a non-renewable resource with no means of storage, so you can only ever access an infinitesimally small slice of it. We call that slice the present. To that end, we can never really become happy. We can only ever be happy, right here, right now.
